title: Building our third algorithmic trading strategy — focusing on validation before profitability
author: BlackGreep
selftext:
We've developed three strategy directions so far, and the latest is \*\*Regime-Adaptive Trend Pullback v0.1\*\*.

The strategy combines:

- EMA20/EMA50 for trend direction
- Pullback detection on M1
- Liquidity sweep and reclaim conditions
- Relative volume confirmation
- ATR-based stop-loss
- A reference 1:2 risk/reward target
- Closed M5/M15 data for higher-timeframe context

We're building the execution and research infrastructure around it rather than relying on indicator signals alone.

Our recent engineering milestones include:

- A synthetic replay pipeline covering signals, order planning, venue normalization, portfolio admission and accounting
- Adversarial testing of terminal portfolio valuation and event ordering
- A one-shot historical replay driver, with 248 related synthetic regression tests passing

\*\*Important:\*\* this is engineering validation, not proof of a profitable strategy. We haven't completed a real historical backtest for Trend Pullback yet.

The next step is connecting an explicitly authorized historical dataset and evaluating the strategy with realistic execution costs.

I'm curious about one thing:

\*\*When evaluating a new algorithmic strategy, what would make you distrust its backtest results the most — overfitting, slippage, data leakage, execution assumptions, or something else?\*\*

I'd be interested in hearing how other systematic traders approach this.

comments.author: itlogicpartnersllc
comments.body: data leakage would be my biggest red flag especially with multi timeframe signals. i would also test out of sample performance across different market regimes before trusting results.

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: The one that makes me distrust a result most is how many versions were tried to get it, since the best of many tries looks good by luck alone. So I'd want the full count of settings and rules tested, and the result judged against that, or against the best of the same number of random strategies. Next would be leakage, like signals using a bar's close before it's known, and then costs, since small errors in slippage matter a lot for a one-minute system. Keeping the final stretch of data untouched until the very end helps with all three. Cymetica's Backtest Labs is one place to run that kind of check with fees and out-of-sample data.

comments.author: QATSAlgo
comments.body:
For this particular M1/M5/M15 setup, I’d first audit the clock: at each M1 decision, which M5/M15 bars were actually closed and available? Then make the sweep/reclaim fill wait until its evidence exists, model spread/fees/slippage and test the adverse ordering when stop and target both fit inside one bar. Keep the parameter-search count and a genuinely untouched test period too. The regression tests establish engineering behavior; they don’t establish an edge, as you say.



We’re QATS. If you later want to test a separate prop execution adapter, try our REST Trading API: [https://quantityproject.github.io/qats-trader-api/](https://quantityproject.github.io/qats-trader-api/) . It exposes account/risk state alongside orders and positions, with persisted idempotency keys for writes and reconciliation after uncertain responses. Our perpetuals evaluations and initial funded accounts are simulated, and plan risk checks still apply; this would be a separate integration, not evidence that the strategy is profitable.
